In this vlog, we are going to build and decorate a gingerbread house.

I used to love to watch my mother cook at Christmas. She would always clear the kitchen table and cover it with a plastic tablecloth. I would help her measure out the ingredients. I used to place each cup of flour, teaspoon of cinnamon and tablespoon of ginger carefully in the bowl.

Yesterday we made the traditional gingerbread dough. I've got a set of pieces here to assemble. I have already made one house as you can see here. I've decorated it with the hard icing, chocolates and of course, the customary pair of candy canes. If you haven't put everything out yet, take the time to do it now.

A lot of people don't eat their gingerbread houses. To me, the only thing better than making a gingerbread house is eating it! On New Year's Day, mother used to cover it with a cloth and smack it with a hammer. My whole family would have gingerbread and tea! Every mouthful was heaven!

Used to and Would to Talk About Past Habits
Used to and would are both used to talk about past actions.
I used to love to watch my mother cook at Christmas.
She would always clear the kitchen table and cover it.

You use used to to say that something happened in the past but doesn't happen any more. It uses -ed to show past tense.

For example: I used to skate every winter.
(Before, I skated every winter, but now I don't skate.)

When we were children, we used to skate all day long.
(Before, we skated all day long, but now we don't skate all day long.)

We use would to talk about both past actions and past routines.

Would refers to actions, rather than situations.

The Present Perfect vs.  The Simple Past Tense
You use the Present Perfect tense when the action has some relationship to now.
Let's look at some other ways to use the Present Perfect.
